# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real customer's name (SITE names client companies; none is used).

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

insights.line: What would have made a difference?

whys.g1: Marcus's answer is about not wanting extra paperwork and transfers, the same operational-burden point as mine, so it fits the 'easy to get at' group; leaving it on its own is one odd placement, even though his wish for a better rate sits awkwardly with the 'not more yield' part of the name.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all three are real answers about where to keep the cash.

founder.order_why: It runs from where I sell, to the context (who, when, window), to the problem, to my solution and its conditions, to the pilot and saving, which is how I'd explain Palus to anyone.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same prompt ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'), so the context step reads as asked twice around the window question on screen 4. Screens 12 and 13 show the same compatibility row (one to two business days) with the same Keel suggestion, once to check and once to choose, which feels like the same question twice.
founder.missing: Price: nothing asks what I charge (a flat 0.25% a year on the balance, against the 0.15–0.60% the bank's treasury product takes) or what yield the company now gives up. Who decides and pays: nothing separates the finance lead who moves the cash from the founder-CEO, and sometimes the board, who signs off on where the reserve sits. Purchase friction: nothing asks what stands between them and buying, such as weeks of diligence on a new provider or a tax adviser's sign-off on the bonds. Also, screen 4 has a typo: 'needded'.

PRIMARY.order_why: Screen 2 asks whether my raise cash sat at the bank's default rate, then screen 5 jumps to 'the most recent time you left money in your bank's treasury product' as if I'd already said I use one, and the one-to-two-day wait on screen 4 comes before I know why I'd care about it.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 5 and 7 both ask whether I'd move to Palus; screens 6 and 8 both get the same answer from me, which is that the operational burden matters more than yield.
PRIMARY.missing: Nothing asked what rate I earn now (about 3.2%) or how much I hold, whether the account is FDIC-swept or insured, how quickly I can get money back for payroll, or who has to sign off on moving it (board or investment policy). Those decide it for me more than yield does.

screens.why5: My two rows, 'Higher yield on cash not needed for months' and 'No treasury hire to manage it', sit on the screen as I typed them, each under nine words.

screens.why1: Right after I said what they'd have to do to start, Keel shows my efforts back for me to check before I pick the one to test, which is the obvious next step.

screens.why1: Right after I checked my effort rows, picking which one strangers will be asked about is the obvious next step.

screens.why1: Asking whether to collect emails from willing respondents fits naturally at the last step before strangers see the study, after the idea and its beliefs are set.

screens.why_b1: The verdict and its deciding number sit together, but the verdict names Relative advantage as 'Not holding up' while Adoption friction below is 'Did not hold', so it doesn't read as 'the worst of all its cards' as the footer claims, and I can't tell which belief actually sank it.
screens.why_b2: Compatibility and Relative advantage read cleanly as 'x of n · bar y of n', but Adoption friction gives two overlapping lines ('3 yes (1 on a condition), 4 do not' and '3 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7 · 2 short · 1 on a condition') that take a second look to reconcile.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names are mine and the beliefs are recognisable, but the solution statement is garbled ('the finance lead the treasury account links…', 'gets back the cash back') and the Relative advantage line is a clumsy splice of my two advantages.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page tells me what to do. It doesn't say whether 4 of 7 balking at moving the reserve means I should lead with a small first move, chase the board and policy blockers, or rethink the yield pitch.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible throughout and nothing is called strong, but no line says seven is a small sample, and 'Not holding up' versus 'Did not hold' implies a distinction the screen never explains.
screens.instead: Did not hold: only 3 of 7 finance leads would move the reserve out of the bank's treasury (bar 5), and just 2 of 6 said it would have gone better. Waiting two days is fine for 6 of 7, so the blocker is moving the money, not liquidity. Open Adoption friction to see what stopped the other four. Seven people is a small read.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said yes, easily or most of the time · bar 5 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers (3, 3, 1, 0), the strip shows the 7 people, and the marker sits at 5 of 7 with the one-in-three rule spelled out, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Compatibility and the belief line is the one I checked: "could wait one to two business days for their cash". The bar line "You said could wait..." is a clipped fragment, but it is still clearly mine.
screens.why_b4: The So line says liquidity timing is not the blocker and points me to Adoption friction, and Lena's quote about the board wanting insured money shows where the real resistance is.
screens.why_b5: The count line hedges with "a small group: a lean, not a call", but the So line then says flatly that the wait "is not what will stop them" and names Adoption friction as the blocker. That is a firmer call than 7 people, half of them only "most of the time", can carry.
screens.instead: So: on 7 people, waiting a day or two looks like it won't stop finance leads (half said only most of the time); the board's wish for insured cash, Lena's point, is worth checking under Adoption friction.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits beside '2 of 6 said it would have gone better', and the So line ties it to 4 of 6 against, past my limit of 2.
screens.why_b2: What is counted and over how many is plain, but 'your bar · 4 of 6' next to '4 of 6 said no difference or worse' makes the bar read like the against count until I parse that it means 4 of 6 must say better.
screens.why_b3: The belief carries both my benefits, but the 'You said' line keeps only higher yield and drops 'no treasury hire to manage it', and the moment is a routine treasury balance, not the time leaving it there cost me.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the count and points to the reasons, but never says what the quotes show: liquidity, insurance and no new paperwork beat a point of yield, so the pitch has to answer safety and access, not just yield.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 with 6 counted is visible, Rachel's 'can't tell' is set apart, and the small group is called a lean, not a call.
screens.instead: Not holding up: only 2 of 6 (both a lot) said Palus would have done better, and I needed 4; the ones who said no difference valued same-day access, FDIC insurance and no extra paperwork over yield, so lead with safety and access before yield.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "3 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7 · 2 short", so I know the verdict and the number that decides it at once.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly counts 7 people's answers, but the bar is given three ways (5 of 7 for, "no more than 1 in 3" against, and "your bar of 2" in the So line), so I had to stop and work out that they mean the same thing.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and "move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury" are the effort I picked, in my own words.
screens.why_b4: "Their reasons are below" points me at the answers but doesn't say what this means for Palus, such as leading with a small trial slice of the reserve rather than asking for the whole reserve, or answering the on-demand-liquidity condition up front.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the screen says it's a lean, not a call, but "4 do not" and "4 of 7 would not move" flatten two "probably not" answers into flat refusals, and "Their reasons are below" promises reasons when only one quote follows.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 3 of 7 would move the reserve (1 only if it stays available on demand), 5 needed; 2 said no and 2 probably not. A small group, so a lean, not a call. Try asking for a small slice of the reserve first, and show same-week access up front.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict word with the deciding count and bar beside it (2 of 6 vs bar 4 of 6, 3 of 7 vs bar 5 of 7, 6 of 7 vs bar 5 of 7), though 'Not holding up' and 'Did not hold' name a similar state two ways.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names are mine and the beliefs are recognisably mine, but the Relative advantage line is a machine-composed sentence ('For most, with it, the last time they left money in their bank's treasury product would have given them...') I would never have written.
screens.why_b4: Beyond the 'When a line fails' header, nothing says what the failed yield and move-the-reserve lines mean for Palus or what to change or test next.
screens.why_b5: Counts and who never saw each question are honest and visible, but every line rests on 6 or 7 people and the screen never says that is a small number, and Lena's insured-money quote sits under the two-day wait as if it explained that line.
screens.why_b6: The themes add to what I typed: these finance leads rank insured and easy-to-get-at above yield, Marcus would take a better rate inside the bank he already has, and Rachel's accountant wants plain cash for the tax break, which is a blocker I had not put in the study.
screens.instead: Yield isn't what these 7 finance leads want; safety, insurance and staying inside their bank are, and a tax adviser can block the move. Lead with safety and same-bank access, and test a small first move with founders before trusting these small counts.

screens.why1: As the first screen it rightly checks I run a startup's cash at a Mercury- or Brex-type bank before asking me anything else.
screens.why2: Mercury and Brex are the banks my peers and I use, so I'd answer this on first hearing.
screens.why3: I run our accounts and cash day to day, so I know where it sits without guessing.
screens.why4: A screener needs only Yes and No, both are clear, and no escape is wanted here.
screens.why5: It names my kind of bank and nothing of anyone's product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It's short and one question, but 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' sounds stiff for a yes/no gate where a plain 'Yes or no.' says it better.
screens.instead: Do you run your startup's cash at Mercury, Brex or a similar startup bank? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I run our cash at Mercury, asking whether our raise money just sat at the bank's default rate is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: "Did you have raise cash earn the bank's default rate" took me a second read; I'd say "did the money from our raise sit at the bank's default rate", and "raise cash" isn't how I'd put it.
screens.why3: I know exactly where our raise money sits and what it earns (about 3.2% on the default sweep), so I can answer from my own books.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it cleanly, but the chip "I can't recall one particular cash from a raise" reads as nonsense next to this question.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or anyone's plan reaches me, just where our cash sat and what it earned.
screens.why6: It's short and ends with a clean "Yes or no", but "did you have raise cash earn" is a stumble heard once.
screens.why7: Yes and No are the gate's two fixed answers with no escape, and both are true of someone (I'd say Yes, while a lead who moved cash into T-bills says No), but the event is a standing state (where the cash sat) rather than what it cost us inside the window, so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did the money from your raise sit at your bank's default rate when it could have earned more elsewhere? Yes · No

screens.why1: Part 2 opens with the idea, and after asking whether my raise cash sat at the bank's default rate, a pitch for earning more on it obviously comes next.
screens.why2: Plaid, custodian, floating-rate, short-duration, government-backed mortgage bonds and money market fund are all words I use every week running our cash, so I get it on one read.
screens.why3: It is about where my own reserve sits and how fast I can get it back to checking, which is exactly what I decide.
screens.why4: A card to read with no options.
screens.why5: It is a deliberate idea card in the founder's three parts with a clear 'the people building it believe', and nothing leaks beyond the product being revealed on purpose; 'long-term reserve' is a little theirs, but I would say 'the cash we won't touch for a year' and know what they mean.
screens.why6: Heard once, the 'how' runs to five sentences instead of one line, 'long-term reserve' comes twice, and 'short-duration, floating-rate and government-backed' is a mouthful of stacked hyphenated terms to hold before the return figures arrive.
screens.instead: Imagine Palus, a treasury account for the reserve you won't need soon. It holds that cash in short-term, government-backed mortgage bonds in your company's name, and gets it back to checking in one to two business days. The people building it believe it would earn 4.5 to 5 percent, against about 3.5 in a money market fund.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, the first thing I would ask about something holding our reserve in bonds is whether I could live with not getting the money back the same day, so it sits well here.
screens.why2: "Your last cash from a raise" is a clumsy way to say "your last raise", and "your cash" makes me stop: all of it, or just the reserve? I could wait two days on the reserve, but never on payroll money.
screens.why3: I move our cash myself, so I know from our own payroll and vendor runs whether a one-to-two-day wait would have hurt.
screens.why4: The four answers are distinct and the escape fits, but "most of the time" and "only sometimes" read oddly against one raise; they only make sense if I picture every time I pulled money out after it.
screens.why5: "One to two business days" keeps the founder's own range, and nothing of the product leaks past the card shown on purpose.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold, though the anchor "your last cash from a raise" sounds a little stiff said aloud.
screens.why7: The four options are on one measure, in the right order, with a working balance and the escape in place, but "your cash" is wider than the long-term reserve the idea actually locks up, so someone who needs operating cash same-day answers against a condition the idea doesn't impose.
screens.instead: Think of your last raise. Could you have waited one to two business days to get your reserve cash back? Yes, easily · Yes, most of the time · Only sometimes · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the settlement-time question, asking whether Palus would have done better than where my reserve sits now is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: I can answer it, but 'money you would not touch' isn't how I'd say it (I'd say reserve or runway), and 'safe and earning' bundles two things that pull apart for me, since mortgage bonds might earn more but feel less safe, so I'd read it twice to know which 'better' to judge.
screens.why3: Our reserve sits in our bank's treasury sweep at about 3.2%, so I know exactly what I'd be comparing Palus against.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it cleanly, and 'I can't tell' is the honest out when safety and yield trade off.
screens.why5: Nothing beyond the card shown on purpose reaches me; 'treasury account' is my own trade's word, and 'the money from a raise' is plain enough even if I'd say 'our raise'.
screens.why6: Two long sentences back to back, the second with 'Palus, a treasury account,' wedged in before 'keep the money from a raise safe and earning better, or not', make a mouthful to hold before the four short options come.
screens.why7: The measure, the four fixed answers in order, the balance and the lone 'I can't tell' are all right, but the anchor is a standing state ('the most recent time you left money... in your bank's treasury product') rather than the moment it cost me, and 'safe and earning' asks about two gains at once.
screens.instead: Think of the last time your reserve sat earning only your bank's default rate. Would Palus, a treasury account, have helped you keep that cash earning better, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: Asking what would actually help after I said Palus wouldn't change much is the obvious next question at the end of the idea part.
screens.why2: The back-reference is fine, but the founder's long phrase 'keeping the money from a raise safe and earning until the company sends it' is pasted in whole; I'd say 'managing our raise cash' and have to reread to get the point.
screens.why3: What would make managing our idle cash better is exactly what I deal with, mostly the operational burden more than the yield.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: 'Sends it' has drifted from the founder's 'spends it', so the job now reads as moving money rather than spending it down, and the founder's own job phrasing reaches me word for word.
screens.why6: It is one question and sayable, but the long pasted clause is a mouthful heard once, and 'until the company sends it' trips the ear.
screens.instead: You said Palus wouldn't make much difference for your last raise. What would make managing that cash easier or better for you, if anything?

screens.why2: 'Long-term reserve' and 'the bank's treasury' are how I talk about the cash we won't touch and Mercury Treasury, so I'd answer on first read.
screens.why3: I decide where the raise sits and I'd be the one moving it, so I can answer from what I do.

screens.why5: Only the idea card's own words reach me ('long-term reserve', 'mortgage bonds'), shown on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan leaks.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four short options and one escape, easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: Moving the reserve is an effort I'd take myself, the fixed four run Yes, Only if, Probably not, No with I can't tell apart, and the belief could go either way.
screens.instead: To use Palus, you'd move part of your raise out of your bank's treasury into a new account. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if it added no work for us · Probably not · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: I just said I wouldn't move the money out of my bank's treasury, so asking why is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: I'd call it our reserve or our runway rather than a 'long-term reserve', and 'too much trouble' assumes my reason when I might just not trust a new place with it.
screens.why3: I know exactly why I keep it at Mercury: one login, one set of approvals, no extra ops for an extra point of yield.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: 'Long-term reserve' reads like the product's term for my cash, and the question decides for me that my no was about hassle and not about safety or trust.
screens.why6: One short question that's easy to hear once and answer.
